fetched_contents.text: Loop Diuretics in Clinical Practice Abstract Diuretics are commonly used to control edema across various clinical fields. Diuretics inhibit sodium reabsorption in specific renal tubules, resulting in increased urinary sodium and water excretion. Loop diuretics are the most potent diuretics. In this article, we review five important aspects of loop diuretics, in particular furosemide, which must be considered when prescribing this medicine: (1) oral versus intravenous treatment, (2) dosage, (3) continuous versus bolus infusion, (4) application in chronic kidney disease patients, and (5) side effects. The bioavailability of furosemide differs between oral and intravenous therapy. Additionally, the threshold and ceiling doses of furosemide differ according to the particular clinical condition of the patient, for example in patients with severe edema or chronic kidney disease. To maximize the efficiency of furosemide, a clear understanding of how the mode of delivery will impact bioavailability and the required dosage is necessary. Keywords: Loop diuretics, Furosemide, Chronic kidney disease Introduction Diuretics are commonly used to control edema in a number of clinical fields. Diuretics reduce sodium(Na+) reabsorption in specific renal tubules, resulting in an increase in urinary sodium and water excretion. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle reabsorbs about 25% of the Na+ of the glomerular filtrate. The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs approximately 5% of the Na+ through a thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride (Na+-Cl-) co-transporter. About 1-2% of the Na+ is transported at the distal segment of the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. Loop diuretics can inhibit the largest amount of Na+ reabsorption by acting on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Furosemide inhibits the sodium-potassium-chloride (Na+-K+-2Cl-) co-transporter in the apical membrane of tubular epithelial cells in the thick ascending limb1). In this article, we review five important aspects of loop diuretics that we must be aware of when we prescribe this medicine: (1) oral versus intravenous treatment, (2) dosage, (3) continuous versus bolus infusion, (4) application in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients, and (5) side effects. Oral versus Intravenous Treatment The bioavailability of furosemide is extremely variable (10-90%). The bioavailability can be improved if it is taken before meals because food can disrupt its absorption2). Furosemide is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, and its peak diuretic effect occurs between 1 and 1.5 hours after oral administration, and between 10 and 30 minutes after intravenous administration. Furosemide (>95%) binds to plasma proteins. Protein-bound furosemide is delivered to the proximal tubule, and secreted via organic transporters that are expressed at the luminal site of action1,2,3). Approximately 50% of the furosemide load is excreted unchanged in urine, and the rest is metabolized into glucuronide in the kidney. Thus, patients with renal dysfunction show a decreased response and increased plasma half-life of furosemide due to the reduction of urinary excretion1,2,3). In patients with severe edema, the effect of furosemide may be altered due to inadequate gastrointestinal absorption. Patients unresponsive to oral furosemide should be switched to intravenous therapy or oral torsemide. The bioavailability of torsemide is predictable. It is extremely well absorbed (80-90%), regardless of the presence of edema, because it undergoes substantial hepatic elimination. The dosage of intravenously administered furosemide is usually half of that of the oral dose; oral bioavailability is approximately 50%(10-90%)2,3,4). Dosage of Loop Diuretics Loop diuretics have a threshold dose; no diuretic effect is shown when the dose is lower than the threshold dose. They also have a dose-responsive effect. The threshold dose of furosemide differs according to the clinical condition of the patient. For example, the threshold dose of intravenous furosemide is 10mg in a population with normal renal function. This increases to 80-160mg in patients with declining renal function5). Therefore, furosemide doses lower than 80mg are not effective in advanced CKD patients. Loop diuretics have a ceiling dose; this is the dose that shows the maximum fractional sodium excretion. Although loop diuretics display dose-response curves, doses above the ceiling dose are only moderately effective. Repeated infusions with the ceiling dose are more effective than increasing the dose of furosemide4). The ceiling dose of intravenous furosemide also varies in different diseases; this dose is 80-200mg in patients with CKD or nephrotic syndrome, and 40-80mg in patients with congestive heart failure or liver cirrhosis. The half-life of the various loop diuretics are not the same: 1-1.5 hours for furosemide and 3-4 hours for torsemide. The half-life of furosemide is prolonged in advanced renal dysfunction, and the half-life of torsemide is doubled in hepatic dysfunction. Torsemide can be administered once daily while furosemide needs to be administered two or three times a day4). Continuous versus Bolus Infusion The bolus therapy of furosemide rapidly increases sodium excretion. However, this excretion is at its maximum for the first 1-2 hours and then it progressively declines1). The peak natriuretic effect with the second dose is 25% less than that of the first dose. Post-diuretic renal sodium and fluid retention are inevitable6). This compensatory sodium retention occurs along the other segments of the nephron that are not related to furosemide. To avoid this compensation, furosemide should be injected at short intervals or infused continuously. Continuous intravenous infusion is more effective than, or in some cases, similar to, intravenous bolus therapy7,8,9). fetched_contents.text: Uncertainty of Physicians and Patients in Medical Decision Making Today patients frequently present to the doctor's office with large amounts of information, obtained from literature searches, web-based data banks, and other sources, with the intent of optimizing their management or even “demanding” a particular treatment strategy. However, although the growth in the amount of data available to patients has been explosive, the information that a patient acquires might not necessarily be correct, appropriate, or easy to interpret for the patient's particular condition. The physician and presumed expert, on the other hand, while bringing the appropriate knowledge and information to the table, will also know that among patients of comparable age and with similar or identical disease presentation, as assessed by currently accepted criteria, only some will respond to a given treatment, and that for the patient under consideration a different treatment strategy actually may have a higher statistical probability of success than the one in which the patient is primarily interested. However, the scientific literature cannot provide answers as to the optimum strategy for any individual patient. Two short vignettes can help highlight the uncertainty present in such scenarios. Example 1 A patient with intermediate risk acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). A 40-year-old woman is referred with a diagnosis of “intermediate risk” AML after presenting with a 3-week history of fatigue, bleeding gums, and pancytopenia. Bone marrow evaluation at the time of diagnosis revealed 45% myeloblasts and an abnormal karyotype consisting of trisomy 8 in 9 of 20 metaphase cells. Molecular studies showed no evidence of FLT3, NPM1, KIT, or CEBPA mutations. The patient undergoes induction chemotherapy with infusional cytarabine and daunorubicin, achieving complete remission. How should this patient be counseled about the pros and cons regarding the risks and benefits of additional chemotherapy versus hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), given that both therapies may offer similar long-term success rates? Example 2 An older patient with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). A 73-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and diabetes is referred with a diagnosis of “high-risk” MDS after presenting with a 6-month history of fatigue, recurrent infections, progressive anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow evaluation reveals a hypercellular marrow with 5% myeloblasts. Cytogenetic studies show del(7q) in 4 of 20 metaphase cells. He indicates that he is interested in curative therapy. How should this patient be counseled on the potential survival advantage offered by HCT compared with nontransplantation therapy? Uncertainty in the Treatment of Malignant Hematology Sir William Osler once noted that “Medicine is the science of uncertainty and the art of probability” [1]. Although true in many areas, nowhere is this statement more true than in the high-stakes setting of malignant hematology, where patients and providers wrestle daily with decisions that juxtapose high-risk therapies with the potential for cure. In example 1, the benefit of upfront HCT is uncertain based on presently available evidence. Indeed, recent studies show that 80% of younger patients with intermediate-risk AML achieve complete remission (CR) with induction chemotherapy, and some 40% may be cured [2]. The data also suggest that more than one-half of patients with intermediate-risk AML who do not undergo HCT in first CR and subsequently relapse may achieve a second CR [3]. The 5-year overall survival after HCT for this subcohort of patients has been reported to be comparable to that among patients undergoing HCT in first CR [3]. However, the clinicians counseling individual patients have no way of knowing a priori if a particular patient will achieve a second CR following first relapse and thus could be spared upfront transplantation. How can physician acknowledge this uncertainty about cure versus no cure at various stages of the leukemia, and about complications with one strategy versus the other? How can physicians convey this information to patients in the clinical encounter and help them understand the prognostic limitations underlying the decision making process? In example 2, an additional important factor is the patient's age. Although allogeneic HCT remains the sole strategy with proven curative potential for MDS, the disease is most prevalent in older individuals, who frequently present with medical comorbidities. Preexisting comorbidities may lead to unacceptable transplant-related toxicity, however; thus, HCT in older patients generally uses reduced-intensity conditioning, which minimizes toxicity but is associated with an increased rate of relapse [4]. Furthermore, even for high-risk MDS, the survival advantage with HCT (in comparison to hypomethylating therapy) may not be manifest until years after HCT [5]. Because treatment with hypomethylating agents may offer a median survival of 2 years, such conservative management is expected to result in the same survival probability over the first 2 to 3 years after diagnosis as seen with a more intensive approach with HCT. However, again, physicians caring for these patients will not be able to surmise, based on present criteria, whether a particular patient might eventually derive a survival benefit from HCT. In addition, and at the core of the decision making process, 2 otherwise comparable patients may place quite a different value on the probability of 1- or 2-year survival without up-front risk-taking versus an up-front riskier procedure that has a chance of a, say, 5-year survival. These hurdles of uncertainty are currently unsurmountable [6]. The original text contains minor grammatical and phrasing issues, such as “We havent mention last dialysis session” and “This might cause confusion about proper medication dosing, but we will proceed with prescribing furosemide anyway.” These can be corrected and rephrased to reflect standard medical-note phrasing and proper tense usage.

- “We have not included the details of his last dialysis session” is more grammatically correct than “We havent mention last dialysis session” [N1-R2][N1-R3].
- “We will proceed with prescribing furosemide” is acceptable, but “we will proceed with administering furosemide” is slightly more precise in a clinical context [N1-R1][N1-R5].

Proper tense and verb usage for clarity:
- The original note mixes present and past-tense phrasing, but in a medical note, past tense is generally preferred for established facts, while present tense is used for current plans and actions [N1-R1][N1-R5].

- “Payment is done” should be “Payment has already been made,” which is more formal and grammatically precise [N1-R1].

Consistent patient-centered phrasing for medical notes:
- Medical notes should be written in a neutral, objective tone that avoids ambiguity while still being readable to other clinicians and patients [N1-R2][N1-R5].
- The phrase “No mention of last dialysis” can be improved to “No mention of the last dialysis session” to make the missing information more explicit [N1-R3].
- The note should also avoid overly casual language and instead use standard medical terminology, such as “proceed with administering furosemide” rather than “proceed with prescribing furosemide” [N1-R1][N1-R5].

Overall, the revised note would read more clearly and professionally while preserving the original intent. The patient’s concern about uncertainty is valid, and the physician’s response should be framed carefully in the communication standards branch [N4-F3].

Clinical context and risks of omitting dialysis information

Dialysis history matters for fluid overload management because dialysis is a major determinant of fluid balance in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Dialysis removes excess fluid and solutes, so knowing the timing, frequency, and response to dialysis helps estimate residual fluid volume, hydration status, and the likelihood of ongoing fluid retention [N3-R1][N3-R5]. In the clinical scenario described, the patient is admitted for fluid overload, which is a common complication of ESRD and dialysis dependence, and dialysis history is therefore essential for accurate assessment [N3-R4][N5-R3].

How missing dialysis data can affect medication dosing:
- Furosemide dosing is highly dependent on renal function and the patient’s clinical context. In patients with advanced CKD, the threshold dose of intravenous furosemide is 80–160 mg, and the ceiling dose is higher than in patients with normal renal function [N2-F2][N2-R3].
- In ESRD, furosemide may need higher doses to achieve diuresis, and the response may be less predictable than in patients with preserved renal function [N2-R2][N2-R3].
- Without dialysis history, the physician cannot determine whether the patient has recently received dialysis, whether dialysis was effective, or whether residual fluid overload is the main driver of current symptoms [N3-R1][N3-R4].

Clinical consequences of proceeding without dialysis details:
- Proceeding without dialysis details increases the risk of underdosing or overdosing furosemide, both of which can worsen outcomes. Underdosing may fail to reduce fluid overload, while overdosing may cause hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, or worsened renal function [N2-F2][N5-R2].
- The patient’s response to diuretics may also be influenced by recent dialysis, so omitting this information can lead to unnecessary repeat or escalation of diuretic therapy [N2-F2][N2-R2].
- In a hospitalized patient, incomplete information can complicate care continuity and increase the risk of adverse events, especially if the patient’s condition changes rapidly [N4-F3].

In short, dialysis history is not optional in ESRD care because it directly affects fluid management and medication dosing. Omitting it increases uncertainty and can lead to suboptimal or unsafe decisions [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

Documentation standards for dialysis history and ESRD care

What documentation should include for dialysis sessions:
- Dialysis documentation should include the patient’s pre- and post-treatment weight, method of access, treatment duration, and any relevant clinical findings [N3-R1][N3-R5].
- For ESRD, documentation should also reflect the need for care/services provided and should include signed/authenticated orders that note the frequency of dialysis treatment and method of dialysis [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- Clinical findings leading to the diagnosis of ESRD should be included in the visit notes, and documentation should be sufficient to support the clinical decision-making process [N3-R2][N3-R3].

How ESRD documentation requirements affect record completeness:
- Medicare documentation requirements for ESRD emphasize that patient medical records should reflect the need for care/services provided, and the listing of records is not all inclusive [N3-R4][N3-R5].
- ESRD documentation standards require providers to submit or have previously submitted the necessary records to be reimbursed for dialysis and transplant services, which implies a higher standard of completeness than routine care [N3-R4][N3-R5].
- In practice, ESRD documentation often requires a checklist-style approach, such as a dialysis flow sheet with pre/post treatment weights, access method, and treatment details [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Implications for billing, care continuity, and legal/quality standards:
- Billing and reimbursement for dialysis services are tied to documentation requirements, so incomplete records can delay payment or result in denied claims [N3-R4][N3-R5].
- Poor documentation can also disrupt care continuity, because other clinicians may not have access to the full clinical picture, including dialysis history and response [N3-R5][N4-F3].
- From a legal and quality standpoint, incomplete records may expose providers to scrutiny during audits or quality reviews, especially when dialysis history is critical for safe management [N3-R5][N6-R3].

In conclusion, dialysis history is a core element of ESRD documentation, and incomplete documentation can affect billing, care quality, and legal risk [N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R3].

Communication standards for explaining incomplete information

How to acknowledge uncertainty without overpromising:
A clear communication standard is to recognize uncertainty directly rather than downplaying or hiding it. In clinical notes, uncertainty should be stated openly and clearly, so the reader understands the limits of the available information [N4-F3]. The physician’s note should not merely say “we proceed anyway,” but instead explain that the decision was made with incomplete information and that this creates a reasonable degree of uncertainty [N4-F3]. This approach avoids overpromising certainty and keeps the reader informed about the basis of the decision.

How to explain why dialysis details matter:
The note should explain that dialysis history is important because it affects fluid balance and medication dosing. Dialysis is a major determinant of fluid status in end-stage renal disease, and omitting dialysis details can make it harder to judge how much fluid remains, whether diuretics will be effective, and whether the patient’s response is likely to change [N2-F2][N3-R1]. In the specific example, the physician should also note that furosemide dosing is highly dependent on renal function and clinical context, with higher threshold and ceiling doses often needed in advanced CKD [N2-F2][N2-R3]. This explanation helps the patient and reader understand why the missing information matters clinically.

How to reassure the patient/reader about next steps:
The communication should balance transparency with reassurance. The physician should state that the plan is proceeding while acknowledging the uncertainty created by missing dialysis details [N4-F3]. At the same time, the note should identify the next steps clearly, such as the staff preparing medication orders and the expectation that the patient’s response will be closely watched [N7][N4-F3]. Reassurance can also come from emphasizing that the team will continue to monitor the patient closely and adjust the plan as needed once more information becomes available [N4-F3].

Overall, the note should be framed as a cautious, evidence-based decision made with incomplete information, not as a definitive or overly confident statement. This matches standard communication standards for uncertainty and incomplete information [N4-F3], and it aligns with the grammar and tone guidance from the medical-note standards [N1-R1][N1-R5].

Underdosing may fail to reduce fluid overload, while overdosing may cause hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, or worsened renal function [N2-F2][N5-R2]. The patient’s response to diuretics may also be influenced by recent dialysis, so omitting this information can lead to unnecessary repeat or escalation of diuretic therapy [N2-F2][N2-R2]. In a hospitalized patient, incomplete information can complicate care continuity and increase the risk of adverse events, especially if the patient’s condition changes rapidly [N4-F3].

## 5) Documentation standards for dialysis and ESRD care
Dialysis documentation should include the patient’s pre- and post-treatment weight, method of access, treatment duration, and any relevant clinical findings [N3-R1][N3-R5]. For ESRD, documentation should also reflect the need for care/services provided and should include signed/authenticated orders that note the frequency of dialysis treatment and method of dialysis [N3-R2][N3-R5]. Clinical findings leading to the diagnosis of ESRD should be included in the visit notes, and documentation should be sufficient to support the clinical decision-making process [N3-R2][N3-R3].

ESRD documentation requirements affect record completeness because Medicare documentation requirements emphasize that patient medical records should reflect the need for care/services provided, and the listing of records is not all inclusive [N3-R4][N3-R5]. ESRD documentation standards also require providers to submit or have previously submitted the necessary records to be reimbursed for dialysis and transplant services, which implies a higher standard of completeness than routine care [N3-R4][N3-R5]. In practice, ESRD documentation often requires a checklist-style approach, such as a dialysis flow sheet with pre/post treatment weights, access method, and treatment details [N3-R1][N3-R5].

## 6) Implications for billing, care continuity, and legal/quality standards
Incomplete documentation can delay payment or result in denied claims because billing and reimbursement for dialysis services are tied to documentation requirements [N3-R4][N3-R5]. Poor documentation can also disrupt care continuity, because other clinicians may not have access to the full clinical picture, including dialysis history and response [N3-R5][N4-F3]. From a legal and quality standpoint, incomplete records may expose providers to scrutiny during audits or quality reviews, especially when dialysis history is critical for safe management [N3-R5][N6-R3].

## 7) Communication standards for incomplete information
When explaining incomplete information, the note should acknowledge uncertainty directly rather than downplaying or hiding it. A clear communication standard is to recognize uncertainty and state the limits of the available information so the reader understands the basis of the decision [N4-F3]. In the specific example, the physician should explain that dialysis details matter because they affect fluid balance and medication dosing [N2-F2][N3-R1]. This helps the patient and reader understand why the missing information matters clinically.

The communication should also reassure the patient/reader about next steps. The physician should state that the plan is proceeding while acknowledging the uncertainty created by missing dialysis details [N4-F3]. At the same time, the note should identify the next steps clearly, such as the staff preparing medication orders and the expectation that the patient’s response will be closely watched [N7][N4-F3]. Reassurance can also come from emphasizing that the team will continue to monitor the patient closely and adjust the plan as needed once more information becomes available [N4-F3].

## 8) Bottom line
The patient’s concern is valid: omitting dialysis history can create uncertainty about proper medication dosing, especially in ESRD where furosemide dosing is highly dependent on renal function and clinical context [N2-F2][N2-R3]. However, the physician’s response should be framed carefully. The note should be revised for grammar and clarity, the clinical importance of dialysis history should be explained, and the communication should acknowledge uncertainty while reassuring the reader about the next steps [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-F3]. In short, the note is on the right track, but it should be made more precise, more complete, and more transparent [N7][N8][N9].
